paper.citation: Murray IR, McAdams TR, Hammond KE, Haddad FS, Rodeo SA, Abrams GD, on behalf of the Group of American Professional Football Physicians. The use of biologics in NFL athletes: an expert consensus of NFL team physicians. Orthop J Sports Med. 2023;11(2):23259671221143778.
paper.abstract: A three-round Delphi consensus of NFL team physicians on the use of biologics, including platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and cell therapies, in NFL athletes. Of 49 statements in the final survey, 47 reached consensus, including a positive effect of PRP on patellar tendinopathy and knee osteoarthritis symptoms and a recommendation that the term 'stem cell' not be used with athletes.
paper.tldr: NFL team physicians reached consensus on 47 statements about biologics: PRP is considered helpful for patellar tendinopathy and knee osteoarthritis symptoms, evidence for cell therapy is limited, and 'stem cell' should not be used with athletes.
paper.methods: A working group of six experts used a scoping review to draft 78 round-one items, which were rated by NFL team physicians over three Delphi rounds. A statement was counted as consensus if at least 75% agreed and fewer than 10% disagreed. Physicians from 26 teams and NFL London agreed to take part, and 24 completed round one.
paper.findings: Consensus was reached on 47 of 49 final-round statements. PRP was endorsed for patellar tendinopathy (75% agreement) and knee osteoarthritis (75%), but consensus was not reached for Achilles, hamstring, adductor, acromioclavicular, sports hernia, ankle syndesmotic or meniscal injuries. Experts agreed that intravenous stem cell infusions lack supporting evidence (85%) and that routine placental/amniotic injections are not supported (75%), while the microfragmented adipose and bone marrow/fat cell knee osteoarthritis items did not reach consensus.
paper.limitations: This is expert opinion using agreement thresholds rather than a systematic evidence review, and the authors note some positions differ from more recent meta-analyses, such as the use of leukocyte-poor PRP for knee osteoarthritis. Only team physicians were surveyed, participants' industry ties may have influenced responses, and the authors acknowledge selection bias.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use these statements as shared positions in counselling athletes: biologics should be delivered under sports medicine or orthopaedic direction, the lack of strong evidence should be disclosed during shared decision-making, and treating physicians should document preparation details. The consensus does not establish efficacy for most biologic uses and is not a substitute for current high-level evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Performance application is indirect: the consensus concerns treatment decisions for injured athletes and does not establish any performance benefit from biologics. Biologic use by NFL players should not be presented as proof of efficacy, a point the authors stress.
paper.rtp: The consensus does not set return-to-sport timelines or criteria after biologic treatment. It states that decisions should follow current best evidence and clinical experience and that the lack of strong evidence should be explained to athletes, so it cannot be used to time return to play after PRP, cell therapy or other biologics.
